title: Abdali's invasions
hookLine: Ahmad Shah Abdali came down through Punjab again and again

cards: Dust on the road from the northwest. A farmer in Punjab straightens up in his field and watches it. He has seen this before.

A huge army is coming down out of Afghanistan, across the rivers, heading for the riches of Delhi. It will pass through his land on the way there and on the way back. And then, some time later, the dust will rise again.
The king at the head of that army was Ahmad Shah Abdali, and Punjab lay across his road.

teach.h: A KING WHO KEPT COMING BACK.
teach.b: Abdali was the king of Afghanistan, and he invaded northern India again and again. Each time, his army marched through Punjab. For the people there, that meant crops taken, towns emptied, captives carried off.
Then the army went home, the land tried to recover, and the army came back. So the Sikhs' question wasn't how to win one battle. It was how to keep going through a storm that returns.
Tradition and history describe their answer. The Dal Khalsa mostly didn't meet the full army head on.
They let it pass, and struck its edges and its rear, especially on the way home, when it was heavy with plunder and captives, the same tactic the riders used on Nadir Shah's army this week.
And when the army left, they came out of the forests and took the countryside again.

Sikhs have a phrase for that spirit, one this path met in the forests, and it comes in the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of gurdwara gatherings: chardi kala. Rising spirits, a spirit that keeps climbing.
The Ardas asks that through the Name there be chardi kala. It isn't cheerfulness. It's the refusal to stay knocked down.
Look back at this week through that lens. A father and son who would not give up their faith. Captives brought home.
Grief held without hate. Villages kept safe. Scattered bands made one army, and a leader who carried his people.

teach.h: A WEEK OF STANDING UP AGAIN.
teach.b: Each was a way of standing up again.
Abdali came again and again. So did they.

how: Sikhs close the Ardas, said at the end of gurdwara gatherings and in daily prayer, by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, through the Name, and tell the stories of the eighteenth-century Khalsa as stories of chardi kala.

games.q: you're with the Dal Khalsa. a huge Afghan army is marching through Punjab toward Delhi. what do you do?
o: meet the whole army head on in the open.
let it pass, strike its edges and its rear, and come back when it leaves.
games.why: tradition and history say the Khalsa mostly struck the edges and the rear, especially on the way home, and took the countryside back each time.

practice: Bring to mind something that keeps coming back in your life, a Sunday-night worry, an argument that circles round, and let yourself be tired of it; that's allowed.
Then breathe in with the word again, and out with and again, not as a complaint but as standing up one more time. If you pray, say Waheguru instead.

wordCard.voice: Abdali's invasions. The Afghan king's armies came through Punjab again and again, and the Khalsa met each return by returning too, in the spirit the Ardas calls chardi kala. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chardi kala, rising spirits, the spirit that keeps climbing; asked for at the close of the Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: again and again. Rising spirits are built one return at a time. Rest well; a new week starts tomorrow.
